title: Weight progression on evolving rep ranges
summary: He explains how to choose weight jumps when using evolving rep ranges. There is no universal number, only a method: jumps depend on the lift, your level and how the range is set up. He gives his own 2.5-5 lb per side rules and his deadlift scheme.
claims: The right weight jump within an evolving rep range depends on your whole program, your training level and the lift; there is no universal answer, only a methodology
Using the same fixed weight jump for squat, bench, deadlift and press makes no sense because each lift progresses at a different rate
Fixed jumps on every lift, as in Starting Strength, only work for beginners and are convenient rather than optimal
When he first made real strength progress he added 10 lb per side (20 lb) to his rep work each time; once he stalled it took him forever to realise the jumps were too big
Avoid microplates or fractional plates unless you are really advanced and it is the only way left to milk progress
Use 2.5 lb per side as the minimum jump; for intermediates the realistic range is 2.5 to 10 lb per side
His rule is 5 lb per hand: 5 lb each side on bench, 2.5 each side for a one-hand barbell hold, same logic for dumbbells
Curls and overhead press are the exceptions: 5 lb per side proved too much and made his strength regress
Because he focuses on higher reps and pushes volume more than intensity as the range evolves, 5 lb per side jumps suit him while 10 would not
Deadlift scheme 2-3-2-4-3-2-5-3-2: once he gets 5, then 4, then 3 reps with a weight, next week he does 2 reps with that weight plus 10 lb
A volume-focused evolving range climbing toward 6-10 reps may need smaller 2.5 lb jumps, because the tonnage gained per set may not justify a bigger jump into the next lower-rep evolution
A tight intensity-focused range such as 1, 2-1, 3-2-1 progresses with more difficulty and may need more variations and lighter pulls, but when it moves you may jump 10 lb
Your body may react differently to rep ranges than his; evolving rep ranges are what you make of them
Decide how you will load plates before choosing the evolving range; if weight progression and range do not correlate, change one of the two
If the same evolving range keeps forcing you to change how you add plates, the range is probably too wide: it spans too big an intensity window and the volume is all over the place
Evolving rep ranges offer freedom but must stay confined within brackets so they still promote progression
